title: Convolutional Neural Network
description: Watch a tiny convolutional network read a hand-drawn digit: filters slide over the pixels, ReLU and pooling shrink the result, and a final layer decides.
youWillLearn: How an image becomes a grid of numbers
What a filter (kernel) is and how it slides across an image
What feature maps, ReLU and pooling do
Why the same small filter can spot a pattern anywhere

story.title: A picture is a grid of numbers
story.body: To a computer this digit is just 64 numbers: 1 where there is ink, 0 where there isn't. A normal network would treat those 64 numbers as unrelated inputs. But pixels have neighbours, and shapes like edges and corners are made of neighbouring pixels.
story.keyIdea: Images have structure: nearby pixels belong together.

story.title: A small filter looks at one patch
story.body: A **filter** (or kernel) is a tiny 3 × 3 grid of weights. Place it on a 3 × 3 patch of the image (blue box), multiply each pixel by the weight on top of it, and add everything up. A big result means the patch matches the filter's pattern. These four filters were learned during training.
story.keyIdea: One filter = one small pattern detector.
story.math: `value = Σ pixel × weight + bias` over the 9 squares.

story.title: Slide it everywhere
story.body: Now slide the same filter one square at a time across the whole image: 6 × 6 = 36 positions. Each position gives one number, and together they form a **feature map**: a map of where in the picture this pattern appears.
story.keyIdea: The same weights are reused at every position, so a pattern is found wherever it is.

story.title: Keep the matches
story.body: Negative numbers mean *this is not the pattern*. ReLU simply sets them to 0 and keeps the positive matches. What remains highlights where the filter fired.

story.title: Shrink it: max-pooling
story.body: Max-pooling cuts the 6 × 6 map into 2 × 2 blocks and keeps only the biggest value of each, giving 3 × 3. The network keeps *whether* the pattern appeared in a region, not its exact square, so small shifts of the drawing matter less.
story.keyIdea: Pooling makes the network more tolerant of small shifts.

story.title: Combine and decide
story.body: All four filters do the same, giving four small pooled maps: 36 numbers in total. A final layer weighs them into one score per digit, and softmax turns the scores into probabilities. The tallest bar is the network's answer.
story.keyIdea: Filters find parts; the last layer puts the parts together into a decision.

done.title: Done
done.body: Draw your own digit in the Lab and watch every number change.

lab.breakIt: Load **Noisy 8**: with 13 of its 64 squares flipped (about 20 %) the network still says 8, but only about two-thirds sure, with 0 close behind. Over many noisy digits its accuracy falls from 93 % to about 53 %, because it only ever trained on light noise. Then erase squares from a clean digit, one at a time, until the answer flips.

sections.heading: What is a convolutional neural network?
sections.body: A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a neural network built for grid-shaped data such as images. Instead of connecting every pixel to every neuron, it slides small **filters** across the image. Each filter is a pattern detector, and because the same weights are used everywhere, a pattern is recognised wherever it appears.

sections.heading: The building blocks
sections.body: **Convolution** slides each filter over the image to make a feature map. **ReLU** keeps the positive matches. **Pooling** shrinks each map so small shifts matter less. Real CNNs stack many such layers: early filters find edges, later ones combine edges into corners, curves and finally whole objects. A final fully-connected layer turns the features into class scores.

sections.heading: This lesson's network
sections.body: The network here is tiny: four 3 × 3 filters, one pooling step and one output layer, about 400 numbers in total. It was trained offline on 4,000 digits generated from a hand-drawn 5 × 7 font, placed at random spots with a few flipped pixels. It reaches about 93 % on new digits of the same kind. Your browser recomputes every step from those weights.

sections.heading: Why convolutions work so well
sections.body: Sharing one filter across the whole image means far fewer weights than a fully-connected layer, and it builds in a useful assumption: a cat's ear looks like a cat's ear wherever it is in the picture. That is why CNNs led the deep learning revolution in image recognition.

faq.a: Nobody: they were learned by gradient descent and backpropagation, exactly like the weights in the earlier lessons. Training discovered which patterns help tell digits apart.

faq.q: Why are the maps smaller than the image?
faq.a: A 3 × 3 filter fits in 6 positions across an 8-wide image (without padding). Pooling then halves the size again.

faq.q: Can a CNN recognise a digit anywhere in the image?
faq.a: Within limits. Shared filters and pooling make it tolerant of small shifts, which is why every digit still works here when shifted anywhere the 8 × 8 grid allows (try **Shifted 3**). Large shifts, rotations or very different styles need training examples like them.

faq.q: Why does a blank canvas say 1?
faq.a: The last layer must share 100 % between the ten digits; it has no "nothing here" answer and never saw an empty grid in training. A blank grid happens to look most like a thin 1 to it, so it says 1, about 90 % sure. Real systems add a "none" class or ignore low-confidence answers.

faq.q: Is this how photo apps recognise faces?
faq.a: The same idea scaled up enormously: millions of weights, dozens of layers, millions of training images, plus newer designs such as residual connections and attention.

byHand.problem: A 4×4 grayscale image has a bright vertical stripe in the middle (1 = bright, 0 = dark); the second grid is a 3×3 edge filter. Slide the filter over the image, apply ReLU, then max-pool the {size} result into one number.

steps.title: The first position
steps.body: Lay the filter on the top-left 3×3 window, multiply each pair of numbers and add all nine products. The result, {first}, is negative: from left to right this window goes from dark to bright.

steps.title: Slide the filter
steps.body: Move one pixel at a time and repeat. The output is a {size} feature map. The right-hand windows give {second}: an edge from bright to dark.

steps.title: ReLU
steps.body: Negative values become 0, so only the bright-to-dark edges survive.

steps.title: Max pooling
steps.body: 2×2 max pooling keeps the largest value in each 2×2 block. Our map is exactly one block.

byHand.answer: The filter found the right edge of the stripe: after ReLU and pooling the output is **{pooled}**.
